Minimum wage is mostly just a red herring. The article mentions being able to replace a human for $35k. That's a machine that can work 24/7. There are just under 9000 hours in a year. Even after you factor in maintenance expenses the only thing keeping humans employed is inertia. It was recently reported that Foxconn just laid off 60,000 and replaced them with robots and Chinese labor isn't exactly going for $15/hour. And that $35,000 already seems very high relative to what the price could be. In any case each year that goes by that $35,000 goes down.. and down... and down. While the cost of human living expenses continues to go up and up meaning the wages necessary for even a very basic existence continue to rise alongside them.

And obviously it doesn't stop at fry flippers and greeters. People radically underestimate the jobs that can and will be automated. A recent proof of concept was testing automation in surgery. I think mostly this is an increasingly clear wakeup call that our socioeconomic system is in need of a reboot.

I think minimum wage is still an important issue, because raising the minimum wage puts a fire under the asses of businesses to take the initial investment towards automation, which they otherwise might have put off another 5 to 10 years. It makes the transition to automation much more abrupt, and produces a huge glut of unemployed people all at once. Automation is going to happen regardless, but we shouldn't be doing things that could potentially make the transition harder on people. Leave the market alone and let it sort things out naturally. It's easier for someone to transition into another line of work when there aren't 5,000,000 other unemployed people with identical skill levels trying to do the same thing at the same time.

I think if you look a bit into the probable future that the minimum wage might not necessarily be accelerating a crisis, but helping ease it in. Fast food is getting hit today. Uber, Lyft, and other companies are now already testing self driving taxis. A group of Google engineers splintered off to form a heavy haul automation system. Transportation is a dead industry walking. Transportation and food prep alone account for about 20% of the entire US labor force. And again, this is still just the beginning. Business types like risk analysis, accounting, finance, and so on - perfect targets for automation. And this is still all just the beginning. Ultimately most jobs will be disappearing in the relatively near future. We may create some jobs in the process, but nowhere near as many as we'll wipe out.

I think these initial 'soft targets' are actually helping ease in the change. Non manufacturing AI is still in a relatively primitive state. The fact we're bringing the technology in before it's mature is helping people become aware of where we're going without having to wait before it's happening on an enormous scale. It's going to be rough times ahead because there already aren't and there won't be jobs for those 5,000,000 people, but it's better to get it over with now than when it's 20 million people and then more to follow. It's going to be a bumpy ride, but I think this will be a nice wakeup call that our current economic system not sustainable.
